# phig rules — by invariant

## conflict

### R01 — holds

A protected destination is never overwritten under any on_conflict policy; the resolver renames around it.

The protected set covers another image's not-yet-moved source and any real file the database does not track. Overwriting either destroys bytes phig cannot restore, so the guard outranks the policy the user asked for.

| | |
|---|---|
| Enforced at | `core/paths.cpp:resolve_conflict` |
| Binds | `organize.copy`, `organize.move`, `organize.plan` |
| Protects | original-file |
| Evidence | witness: `OrganizeEngineTest.OverwritePolicyStillRenamesAroundAnExistingFile` |

### R02 — holds

A move to an occupied destination fails rather than replacing what is there, whatever the conflict policy decided.

This guard sits below the planner and answers a question the plan cannot: a file that appeared at the destination after planning, from a concurrent phig run or a sync app. It uses the kernel's atomic no-replace rename where one exists, then a hard-link emulation, so the check and the rename are one operation rather than two.

| Enforced at | `core/paths.cpp:move_file`, `core/paths.cpp:rename_noreplace` |
| Binds | `organize.move`, `remove.trash` |
| Protects | original-file, attachment |
| Evidence | witness: `MoveFileTest.RefusesToOverwriteExistingDest`, `MoveFileTest.CrossDeviceRefusesToOverwriteExistingDest`, `OrganizeExecTest.MoveRefusesAnOccupiedDestinationWithoutAuthorization`, `RemoveExecTest.TrashTwoSameNameFilesGetDistinctPathsNoClobberAndLogs` |

### R03 — holds

A destination already claimed by an earlier file in the same run is a conflict even when nothing occupies it on disk.

Two selected files can expand to one destination under the same format string. The first has not been written yet when the second is resolved, so no on-disk check can see the collision; only the claimed set can.

### R05 — holds

The copy branch renames an occupied destination aside before writing and puts it back if any step fails.

Defense in depth: the planner protects every existing on-disk path, so in normal use the destination is free, and this covers any caller that targets an occupied one anyway. The backup is a same-directory rename rather than a byte copy, so every failure path can restore it, and a failed restore is thrown rather than swallowed because the original then sits only at the backup path.

| Protects | original-file |
| Evidence | witness: `OrganizeExecTest.CopyRestoresPriorFileOnDbFailureOverwrite`, `OrganizeExecTest.CopyOverwriteSuccessLeavesNoBackup` |

### R06 — holds

An authorized replace renames the occupant aside before the move and restores it if any later step fails.

move_file refuses to overwrite, so an occupied destination has to be cleared before the rename can succeed; doing it with a same-directory rename means the disk action, the path update and the log entry can all be undone. The backup is removed only after the transaction commits, which is the point at which the replacement the caller authorized has actually happened.

### R08 — violated (test gap)

A run started with on_conflict overwrite replaces the file at an occupied destination.

The flag offers three values and the code has two behaviors. The planner's is_protected returns true for any path that exists on disk and resolve_conflict renames around a protected destination, so a run-level overwrite differs from rename only on an intra-run collision. A user who asks to replace a file gets a renamed copy instead and is not told. R01 records the guard that produces this and is correct on its own terms; what is wrong is that the policy name promises something the guard never allows.

### R09 — holds

An explicit per-item override may replace a file that exists on disk, but never another image's not-yet-moved source.

An override is the caller answering a conflict the plan showed, which is the opposite of the silent loss the on-disk arm of the guard exists to stop, so that arm is bypassed. A batch source is a tracked original phig is in the middle of relocating; no caller intent makes destroying it correct, so an override that lands on one is refused rather than honored.

### R10 — holds

A destination that became occupied between plan and apply is skipped, never re-resolved to a name the caller was not shown.

Re-running the resolver at execution time could file the photo under a name that appeared in no plan, which defeats the point of authorizing one. Skipping keeps the outcome a subset of what was shown, and the item lands in the skipped count so the caller can re-plan and see the new conflict. An item carrying an explicit override is exempt, because that override is the authority to replace what is there.

| | |
|---|---|
| Enforced at | `core/organize_engine.cpp:OrganizeEngine::apply` |
| Binds | `organize.copy`, `organize.move` |
| Protects | original-file |
| Evidence | witness: `OrganizeEngineTest.ApplySkipsAnItemWhoseDestinationBecameOccupied`, `OrganizeEngineTest.ADestinationThatBecameFreeIsSimplyWritten` |

### R11 — holds

A file whose resolved destination is its own path is left alone: nothing is written and nothing is logged, a resolution only the overwrite policy produces.

resolve_conflict's occupancy test has no self-exemption, so a file already sitting at its destination reads as taken and never takes the free-path branch. Only the overwrite arm then returns the path unchanged, because the is_protected predicates do exempt a file's own source; under rename the resolver falls into the suffix loop and files the photo beside itself under a _1 name, and under skip it returns empty. On the path that does reach the executor the guard is what stops a move renaming a file onto itself and logging a meaningless entry, and stops the copy branch running its backup-then-copy dance against the very file it is copying.

| | |
|---|---|
| Enforced at | `core/organize_exec.cpp:execute_organize_action` |
| Binds | `organize.copy`, `organize.move` |
| Protects | original-file, activity-log |
| Evidence | witness: `OrganizeExecTest.NoOpSelfMoveDoesNothingAndLogsNothing`, `OrganizeExecTest.NoOpSelfCopyDoesNotCorruptFile`, `ResolveConflictTest.SelfSourceNotProtected` |

### R69 — violated (test gap)

Writing a command's results to the path named by --output does not destroy what is already at that path.

It does. cmd_search and cmd_duplicates hand the path to a default std::ofstream::open, whose mode truncates, and there is no --on-conflict for --output, no prompt, no backup and no activity-log entry, so the destroyed bytes leave no record anywhere. There are four such open sites, not one: cli/main.cpp:584 in cmd_duplicates, and :962, :991 and :1040 in cmd_search's person, face and general branches, so a fix written against one of them leaves the other three truncating. Measured against a scratch two-image collection with the built binary, a 14-byte file reading IRREPLACEABLE came back as search results from 'phig search --output' (exit 0, nothing on stdout), as duplicate groups from 'phig duplicates --output' (exit 0), as a path and a Found 1 images line from 'phig search --person Alice --output', and as 'Found 0 matching faces' from 'phig search --face <image> --output'. What was there is gone in every case; the sizes are not quoted because they are not properties of the rule — each of those outputs prints collection paths, so its length follows where the scratch collection lives. A search that matches nothing truncates the file the same way — '--ext nosuchext' left 15 bytes reading 'Found 0 images'. 'fav list --output' is the same code, since cmd_fav's list branch fills a SearchOptions and calls cmd_search (cli/main.cpp:1749); it reaches the :1040 site only, and measured, it left the same 15 bytes. Two cases leave the file alone on a run that exits 0. --count prints the count and returns before any stream is opened, on all three search branches (cli/main.cpp:950-952, :983-985 and :1032-1035), so 'phig search --count --output' left the 14-byte file at 14 bytes and did nothing else with the flag, and 'fav list --count --output' did the same. And a person search that matches nobody prints its No images found line and returns at cli/main.cpp:954-957, before the :962 open — measured, 14 bytes unchanged, exit 0. cmd_duplicates has no equivalent: with nothing to report it truncates all the same, '--type exact' against a collection with no exact duplicates leaving 85 bytes of empty summary. The other survivals are error paths that exit 1 — either command's empty-database guard, and a --face query image phig cannot decode or finds no face in. Whether a command destroys the file at --output therefore turns on flags that have nothing to do with output. Every other write phig makes refuses an occupied destination — the resolver renames around a protected one (R01), move_file refuses at the syscall (R02), and a carried attachment refuses outright (R41) — so this is the one write path with no resolution at all. Anchored at cli/main.cpp deliberately: no core/ primitive renders a result to a file, so both the write and any guard on it exist only in the CLI and no other surface could inherit a fix; libphig returns records and leaves the writing to its caller. Plan 060 owns it. The shape is 060's thesis exactly — the run finishes, reports success, exits 0, and something that mattered is gone with no signal and no record — and what has to be decided is whether a successful run may destroy silently, which is a data-safety question rather than the parser question 043 handles. The fix lands in cli/, so it carries the same scoping question 060's open question 3 already raises for cmd_organize's exit code.

| Evidence | subprocess: none |

Every fact above was measured by running the built binary. Only a subprocess test could pin it, on the model of RemoveExecTest.CliRefusesNonInteractiveConfirmationEvenWithPipedYes. |

## reconcile

### R12 — holds

A tracked path is deletable only when its file is gone and its parent directory still exists; a missing parent and a failed existence check are reported apart from it and kept.

A missing file alone does not say what happened. A missing parent directory usually means an unmounted or unreachable subtree rather than a deletion, and an existence check that errors says nothing at all. The three cases warrant different treatment, so the classifier returns them separately and leaves the judgement to the caller instead of collapsing them into one filtered list.

### R15 — holds (test gap)

Scan skips its whole destructive phase when every tracked row under the scanned directory classifies as deletable.

An unmounted drive is indistinguishable from a deleted collection at the point reconcile runs, and losing a whole subtree's tags and faces to a forgotten mount is worse than leaving stale rows behind. The guard compares the deletable set against every row under the prefix, so it fires only when the two are the same size. A run that also has rows in parent_missing or check_failed does not trip it, and its deletable rows are deleted: those other rows are held by the per-row classifier of R12, not by this guard. The guard is coarse on purpose, and it names the flag that overrides it.

### R16 — holds

A stale row's user metadata transfers only when exactly one other tracked file with the same sha256 exists on disk; with none or several it transfers nowhere and the row is still deleted.

With two identical-content files on disk phig cannot tell which one the user moved, and guessing would attach the tags to the wrong photo. The cost of refusing is real and is recorded rather than hidden: the row is deleted either way, and the restore snapshot captures neither tags nor faces, so ambiguity destroys them. Choosing a target is a feature nobody has designed, not an override of this rule.

## atomicity

### R28 — holds

Every write transaction opens with BEGIN IMMEDIATE, so a transaction that reads and then writes cannot fail with SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT.

SQLite in WAL mode pins a read snapshot at the first read of a deferred transaction; if another connection commits before this one writes, the upgrade fails with SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT, which the busy handler does not retry — so the 30-second busy_timeout does not help and the write simply fails. Taking the write lock at BEGIN turns that failure into a wait. Every read-then-write path in the engine has this shape: delete_paths_logged reads a row to snapshot it before deleting it, log_prune scans operations before deleting them, and init_schema reads the version before writing it.

| | |
|---|---|
| Enforced at | `core/database.cpp:begin_transaction`, `core/database.cpp:delete_paths_logged`, `core/database.cpp:log_prune`, `core/database.cpp:insert_batch`, `core/database.cpp:init_schema` |
| Binds | `scan.walk`, `scan.reconcile`, `organize.copy`, `organize.move`, `remove.trash`, `remove.hard`, `remove.db-only`, `remove.orphans`, `relink.transfer`, `relink.demote`, `relink.demote_live_photo`, `metadata.write`, `faces.rebuild`, `faces.identify` |
| Protects | db-row, user-metadata, activity-log |
| Evidence | witness: `DatabaseConcurrency.BeginTransactionTakesWriteLockImmediately`, `DatabaseConcurrency.DeferredBeginCanBusySnapshotOnReadThenWrite` |

### R29 — holds

Each schema migration takes the write lock before it reads the version and re-reads the version inside that transaction, so a step another process already applied is skipped rather than re-run.

The migrations are not idempotent — ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN fails the second time — so two first runs starting together would otherwise both apply the same step and one would die. Re-reading inside the IMMEDIATE transaction means the loser sees the winner's version and moves on. The two schema-creation paths have the same shape for the same reason: each creates every table and sets the version in one transaction, so a crash partway cannot leave a versionless partial schema that the next run misreads as pre-migration.

| | |
|---|---|
| Enforced at | `core/database.cpp:init_schema` |
| Binds | `scan.walk`, `scan.reconcile`, `organize.plan`, `organize.copy`, `organize.move`, `remove.trash`, `remove.hard`, `remove.db-only`, `remove.orphans`, `thumbs.rebuild`, `faces.rebuild`, `faces.identify`, `relink.transfer`, `relink.demote`, `relink.demote_live_photo`, `metadata.write` |
| Protects | db-row, user-metadata, activity-log |
| Evidence | witness: `DatabaseConcurrency.ConcurrentMigrationIsSafe` |

### R30 — holds (test gap)

Reconcile's relink and demote passes commit one row at a time and its deletes commit as a single transaction, so an interruption between them leaves the copied fields on both rows — tags always, gallery when the target had none — the transferred faces on the target alone, and every stale row still present.

The two halves have different failure costs. A transfer copies two of its three fields and moves the third: transfer_user_metadata unions tags onto the target and fills an empty gallery, leaving both in place on the source, while its faces clause is UPDATE faces SET image_id = ?, a move that strips the source row when it fires (R37). So a per-row commit that stops halfway leaves the copied fields duplicated and the faces on the target only, and neither state costs a label — the next scan re-derives the duplication and then deletes the stale row, and the moved faces already sit on the row that pass designated as the survivor. The deletes are the destructive half and go in one transaction, so a stopped run has dropped every stale row or none of them. The ordering between the passes is load-bearing and is pinned: relink runs before demote, so a shared target takes the moved row's gallery rather than the demoted JPEG's.

| Binds | `scan.reconcile`, `relink.transfer`, `relink.demote`, `relink.demote_live_photo` |
| Protects | user-metadata, db-row |

### R31 — holds (test gap)

log_begin_operation commits its operation row on its own before the first entry, so an interrupted run leaves an operation behind — marked interrupted by rm and by reconcile when the failure is an exception, and left in_progress when the process dies.

Opening the operation outside the work's transaction is what makes the row survive a rollback: delete_paths_logged rolls back its own transaction on failure and the operation row stays, so the run is not invisible. The cost is that the terminal status is a second write. Only two of the three callers close the loop: cmd_rm and run_reconcile catch, mark the operation interrupted on a best-effort basis and rethrow, while OrganizeEngine::apply has no such wrapper at all — it catches per file and still writes completed, which is R27's finding. A process that dies instead — a signal, a crash, the machine going away — leaves in_progress under every caller; plan 020 recorded that when it wrote log_finish_operation, noting the state is harmless for its own slice and meaningful for the deferred viewer that still does not exist.

### R32 — holds

OrganizeEngine::apply moves or copies one media file, then commits that file's path update and log entry in a single transaction and compensates if it fails, before starting the next — so a run that stops partway leaves every media file before the stop point moved and recorded and every one after it untouched.

A rename cannot go inside a SQL transaction, so the disk action happens first and outside: move_file runs, then begin_transaction covers only update_path_in_txn and log_add_entry. What makes the pair behave as a unit is compensation rather than a shared transaction — a database failure moves the file back, and a failed move-back is thrown with both paths named rather than swallowed, because the file then sits somewhere no row names. The unit is the media file alone: carry_sidecars runs after execute_organize_action has returned and its transaction has committed, so an attachment moved for that file is outside this boundary and is R33's window, not this rule's.

### R33 — holds (test gap)

A change that touches only the disk — trashing a file, hard-deleting it, carrying a sidecar or an attached JPEG — is written to disk first and logged afterwards in its own autocommit, so an interruption between the two leaves the change done and unrecorded.

A rename and a SQLite commit cannot be one transaction, so one of them goes first, and these paths put the disk action first. Nothing compensates for the gap: execute_organize_action moves a file back when its database write fails, and execute_trash_action and carry_sidecars have no equivalent — if log_add_entry throws, the file stays where it was put and the log does not mention it. For trash that means a file sitting in the trash directory under a random-hex name with nothing recording where it came from, which is the one case where the name alone does not say.

### R34 — unenforced (test gap)

A committed transaction survives a process crash but not necessarily an operating-system crash or a power loss: the connection runs WAL with synchronous=NORMAL, which does not fsync the write-ahead log at every commit.

This is the durability the pragma buys and the cost it accepts, and no plan states either. The consequence is bounded rather than arbitrary: move_file and atomic_copy_file fsync the file and its parent directory before the rename, so the bytes are on disk even when the row naming them is not, and the state a power loss can leave — the file at the destination, the row still naming the source — is the one execute_organize_action's compensation already handles and a rescan reconciles. Recorded because a reader who sees BEGIN IMMEDIATE everywhere will otherwise assume commits are durable against everything.

### R48 — violated (test gap)

A copy or move counts each selected item once: an item is reported as applied or as failed, never as both.

The half-done state behind this is a media file that moved and an attachment that did not. OrganizeEngine::apply increments applied and files_written the moment execute_organize_action returns, then calls carry_sidecars inside the same try. A throw from the carry lands in the catch that increments errors, so an item whose photo moved, committed and logged is counted in both totals, and the error text names the parent as the thing that failed with the attachment's destination inside the message. The item is genuinely half done — R41 is what makes the carry throw rather than destroy, and R33 records that a carried file is logged outside the parent's transaction — so a caller needs to be told which half; instead applied and errors both go up and their sum exceeds the actionable count the progress ticks are denominated against. Measured with the built binary: a cp of one photo whose sidecar destination was occupied printed Done: 1, Skipped: 0, Errors: 1 with a [2/1] progress tick, exited 0, and left the destination row and the copy entry for the parent in place. Plan 060 owns it, the same shape as R27 and R60: an operation that finishes, reports success and exits 0 while its own counters are wrong about what happened.

### R62 — partial (test gap)

No C++ exception crosses an ABI entry point.

Where a phig_ctx* is in scope the body is wrapped in PHIG_TRY/PHIG_CATCH, which converts an exception into a status plus a thread-local message: LockBusy to PHIG_ERR_BUSY, any other std::exception to PHIG_ERR_DB, anything else to PHIG_ERR_INTERNAL. PHIG_TRY expands to a null check on ctx, so the ctx-less entry points cannot use it and wrap their bodies in a plain try/catch(...) instead — phig_init does, and so do twelve of settings.cpp's thirteen. The exception is phig_settings_free, a bare { delete s; } with no handler, counted below among the 39. The hole is the entry points that return something other than phig_status. Scripted over phig.h's 69 PHIG_API declarations, 39 have no handler of their own. Most are trivially non-throwing accessors, or delegate to a wrapped helper — phig_op_copy_start and phig_op_move_start both call start_apply, which uses PHIG_TRY. But phig_query_add_tag push_backs a std::string, the ten phig_query_set_* functions assign one, and phig_op_poll copies the path and error strings, so each can throw std::bad_alloc into a C caller with no way to catch it. No plan states this.

|---|---|
| Enforced at | `libphig/internal.h:PHIG_TRY`, `libphig/internal.h:PHIG_CATCH`, `libphig/context.cpp:phig_init` |

| Protects | db-row, client-process |
| Evidence | witness: `AbiOperations.FailedOperationReportsItsMessageAndRefusesAResult`, `AbiMutate.EachThreadSeesOnlyItsOwnError`, `Abi.InitFailsOnUnopenableDatabase` |
| Test gap | The listed tests show a thrown exception arriving as a status and a message on the wrapped paths. Nothing exercises an unwrapped entry point under allocation failure, which is the only way to reach the hole, and nothing enumerates the entry points to check each has a handler — the count of 39 came from a script run while writing this record, not from a gate. |

### R64 — holds (test gap)

Adding a symbol bumps PHIG_ABI_VERSION_MINOR and the CMake VERSION, and never SOVERSION.

SOVERSION is the major alone, so an additive, backward-compatible change keeps the soname and existing callers need no rebuild; only an incompatible change bumps SOVERSION and MAJOR. The two numbers are hand-maintained in two files and agree today — phig.h has MAJOR 1 and MINOR 3, libphig/CMakeLists.txt has VERSION 1.3.0 and SOVERSION 1, with a comment there saying it must track the header. CI compares them on every push: scripts/rules.py's check_abi_version reads MAJOR and MINOR out of the header and VERSION and SOVERSION out of the CMake file and fails when the three disagree, which phig_abi_version() cannot do — it packs the two header macros together, so a test comparing it to the header cannot see that either has drifted from the CMake value. What no check reaches is the trigger. Adding a symbol needs no edit to the export lists, which match on the phig_ prefix rather than on a list of names, so a new entry point ships exported with both numbers untouched and every comparison still agreeing. The version bump is the only manual step and therefore the only one that can be forgotten.

Nothing counts exported symbols against the minor, so the other half still rests on whoever remembers. Adding a phig_foo() to the header and bumping nothing does trip check 4 — measured against a mirror of the tree — but it stops the author once and sends them somewhere else: 'ABI symbol phig_foo is claimed by no operation and is not in read_only_abi — classify it in rules/operations.toml'. ### R72 — holds (test gap)

A run that will detect faces establishes that it can detect before it writes anything: the OpenCV it was built against must be able to run the detection model, and both model files must be present.

Both engines build every FaceDetector up front — ScanEngine::run_workers before the first file, FacesEngine::run after selection and before the first worker — so a constructor that throws costs the run and nothing else. Deferring either check to the first detection would not: the workers are already committing batches by then, and parallel_for_each stops every worker on the first exception, so the failure would arrive on top of a partly written scan. Ubuntu 24.04 ships 4.6.0, which is why the guard exists rather than being a theoretical case. The check is compile-time because the linked OpenCV is fixed when phig is built, and it runs ahead of the models check because below the floor the models are beside the point: telling that user to download them would send them the wrong way.

### R18 — holds (test gap)

A log entry describing a database change is inserted inside the same transaction as that change, so the log never records a change that did not commit.

The log is the only account of what an operation did, and an account that disagrees with the database is worse than none, because a future undo would restore against a state that never existed. Every writer has the same shape: open a transaction, make the change, add the entry, commit — so a rollback takes the entry with it. delete_paths_logged widens the idea to a batch, with one BEGIN IMMEDIATE covering every row it deletes and every purge_row entry it writes.

### R27 — violated (test gap)

## metadata

### R35 — holds

A re-scan of an already-indexed path updates that row in place rather than replacing it, so the row keeps its id and the tags, favorite and gallery attached to it.

INSERT OR REPLACE deletes the row before inserting the new one, and with foreign_keys=ON that cascades image_tags and faces away and hands the file a new id, so every re-scan would silently strip the one thing a re-scan cannot rebuild. ON CONFLICT(path) DO UPDATE keeps the id and rewrites only the derived columns — hash, phash, dimensions, metadata blob, effective date — and gallery is not in the SET list at all, so a re-scan cannot clear it. The favorite flag needs no clause of its own because it is a row in image_tags like any other tag. Plan 022 finding #1 made this change. Measured with the built binary: tagging a file, favoriting it, setting its gallery and then re-scanning with --force left the tag, the favorite, the gallery and the row id exactly as they were.

A face box and its embedding describe pixels, so once the bytes change they describe pixels that no longer exist and repositioning them is not possible; dropping them is the only honest option and a later `face rebuild` or a `--force faces` scan replaces them. The other half matters more: a person label is user-authored and nothing can reconstruct it, so an unchanged file must not lose one to an ordinary re-scan, and `--force hash` alone must not either — the test is the hash, not the flag. run_workers depends on that: it re-adds this run's detections only when db_.has_faces is false, so a row that kept its faces does not also collect a duplicate set.

### R37 — holds

A metadata transfer unions the source's tags onto the target, fills the target's gallery only when it has none, and moves the source's faces onto it only when the target has none; the source's tags and gallery are left in place.

The three fields fail differently, so they are resolved differently. Tags are a set and a union loses nothing, and the favorite flag rides along because it is a tag. A gallery is a single value, so one of the two has to win, and the target's is the later statement of intent — the user assigned it to the row that still has a file. Faces are the same choice with a sharper edge: detections already on the target came from the pixels that are still there, so stale boxes must not displace them, and the count is checked in C++ rather than as a NOT EXISTS in the UPDATE, which would see the rows it had just moved and stop after one. Faces are also the one field that leaves the source changed. The clause is UPDATE faces SET image_id = ?, a move rather than a copy, so a transfer that fires strips the source row of its faces — DatabaseTest.TransferUserMetadataMovesTagsGalleryFaces asserts exactly that. Each caller commits its own transfer alone, and the source row is deleted afterwards in a separate transaction that run_reconcile opens once every pass has finished, so a source row stripped of its faces and not yet deleted is a state the database really passes through and an interrupted run can leave standing; R38 is the ordering and R30 is the rule that owns what an interruption in that window leaves behind. The window costs no label: the faces sit on the row the pass designates as the survivor, and the next scan finishes the deletion. Measured by forcing the window by hand — moving a labelled face to the target and leaving the source row in place — then re-scanning, which removed the source row and left the face and the name alice on the target. The statement names what is left in place because a caller that transferred between two rows it meant to keep would find the source stripped, and no other rule would tell it.

### R39 — holds

When a moved row and a demoted JPEG both transfer into the same surviving row, the moved row's gallery is the one that lands, because relink runs before demote and a gallery transfer fills only an empty target.

The case is ordinary: a RAW moves on disk and a JPEG sits beside its new location, so relink_moved_rows and demote_jpeg_rows both target the RAW's row. Every other field is order-independent — tags union, and faces move only into a row with none — so the whole of the ordering's visible effect is which gallery survives. The order is the one that keeps the user's own relocation authoritative: the moved row is the same photo the user filed, while the demoted JPEG is an attachment being folded in. Nothing in the code declares the dependency, so it is pinned by tests at both levels and stated here; the counts are identical either way, which is what makes it easy to invert by accident.

## attachments

### R41 — holds

A carried attachment never overwrites an occupied destination, on copy as well as on move.

move_file declines and throws, but atomic_copy_file ends in a rename that replaces silently. An attachment has no row, so a destroyed one leaves no restore snapshot and no error — the run reports Errors: 0. An attachment's destination is derived from its parent's rather than chosen, and the conflict planner never sees it, so there is no skip/overwrite/rename policy to consult and nothing renames it aside: refusing is the only available answer. The guard sits at all three carry sites — metadata sidecars, a Live Photo's video, a RAW's attached JPEG — because they end in the same two primitives. Measured with the built binary: a cp whose planned destination directory already held the parent's .xmp left that file's contents intact and reported the failure.

## concurrency

### R07 — holds (test gap)

A read-then-write on a face row labels only the face it compared: an id whose face was deleted in the gap is out of circulation and matches nothing, and `person_id IS NULL` refuses a face another labeler named first.

The face subcommands and libphig's faces operation both run lock-free, so a lock excludes only other lock-takers and identify's phase-2 write has to defend itself. The predicate is `UPDATE faces SET person_id = ? WHERE id = ? AND person_id IS NULL AND embedding = ?`, and `id = ?` is what carries the deletion case: schema v8 made faces.id AUTOINCREMENT (R51), so a candidate a concurrent rebuild deleted in the phase-1-to-phase-2 gap takes its id out of circulation, and the write matches no row rather than landing on whichever face replaced it. Reproduced against the system libsqlite3 3.51.0 phig links: three candidates read as ids 21, 22 and 23 were deleted, their replacements were issued 24, 25 and 26, and the three writes labeled zero rows — with the embedding clause and without it. `person_id IS NULL` is the clause still doing live work: it makes this a compare-and-set against another labeler, which matters because two lock-free paths can reach the same candidate, and deleting it is the one edit to this predicate that fails IdentifyTest.AnUnchangedFaceIsStillLabeled. `embedding = ?` is belt-and-braces against a state phig cannot reach — R71. A losing write updates zero rows rather than throwing, which is why `labeled` counts changed rows and not statements issued.

### R49 — holds (test gap)

The advisory writer lock excludes only processes that construct one on the same file: no read takes it, and it never excludes a writer that takes none.

WriterLock is an flock(2) on a sidecar file, held for the object's lifetime and released by the kernel on process death, so there are no stale locks to clear. Advisory is the whole shape of the guarantee — every promise it makes is a promise about lock-takers, which is why the face subcommands and libphig's operations can run beside it by design rather than by accident. core/ defines the class and constructs one nowhere; the ten call sites are branches of cli/main.cpp, and libphig constructs one only around its five metadata writes. Measured with the built binary while a separate process held the flock on ~/.local/share/phig/phig.db.lock: search --count, duplicates, face list and tag list all completed normally, and so did a mutating 'phig face rebuild', while thumbs rebuild, rm and tag add were refused under --no-wait with 'Another phig operation is running'.

### R50 — violated (test gap)

A mutating command's advisory lock is taken on the lock file belonging to the database that command is about to write.

It is not. lock_path() takes no argument and returns default_db_path() + '.lock', and cli/main.cpp's acquire_writer_lock calls it after --db has already been parsed, so every CLI command locks the default collection's sidecar whatever database it was given — while libphig locks ctx->db_path + '.lock'. Measured with the built binary, both directions: 'phig --no-wait tag add' against a scratch database succeeded while a separate process held the flock on that database's own .lock file, and the same command was refused with 'Another phig operation is running' while that process instead held ~/.local/share/phig/phig.db.lock. So the CLI serializes commands that share no database, and fails to exclude an ABI caller on the database it was actually given. Plan 029 contains both halves and they disagree with each other: its acceptance criteria say the lock is per-machine and per-DB, and its implementation step defines lock_path() as default_db_path() + '.lock'. 029 is completed and cannot own the fix. Plan 039 names core/lockfile.cpp ('Rewrite') and core/paths.cpp ('Platform split') as files it touches, which is where WriterLock and lock_path() live, so it owns lock_path()'s core/ half; it excludes cli/, though, so acquire_writer_lock's call site — the other half of this rule, and the one that actually has to pass the parsed --db path through — is not 039's to fix. The call site's difficulty is sharper than 'pass the path through' suggests: default_db_path() is itself overridable, and set_path_overrides is fed cfg.db, the config file's value, at cli/main.cpp:1829 — the parsed --db never reaches it. So the lock file follows the config-resolved default and --db has no bearing on it at all. Measured with XDG_DATA_HOME redirected: 'tag add --db /tmp/lk/scratch.db' created <XDG_DATA_HOME>/phig/phig.db.lock and no scratch.db.lock. Two commands given the same non-default --db therefore do still serialize, both on the wrong file; what the rule loses is exclusion against anyone holding the lock that belongs to the database being written, which is what libphig takes.

### R51 — holds

A face id names the same face for as long as that face exists: faces.id is AUTOINCREMENT, so a deleted id is never handed to a later insert.

A plain INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is the rowid and is assigned max(rowid)+1, so deleting the highest face gives its id to the next insert — and a full face rebuild deletes and reinserts at the tail of this table for the whole collection, which makes that the steady state rather than a corner case. AUTOINCREMENT costs one sqlite_sequence row and buys the property the three lock-free face paths lean on. Schema v8 both creates the table that way and migrates an existing one by copying rows into faces_new with their ids preserved, deliberately leaving vec_faces untouched because it is keyed on faces.id and is a vec0 virtual table the copy cannot reach. Two comments in core/ still describe the pre-v8 world and are now wrong: core/faces_engine.h and core/database.h each say faces.id is 'INTEGER PRIMARY KEY without AUTOINCREMENT' and explain the surrounding defences as compensating for reuse that no longer happens. cli/main.cpp's cmd_face comment has the current version.

### R52 — holds (test gap)

A face rebuild reads an image's id inside the same transaction that writes that image's faces, so an image deleted while the worker waits for the write lock costs one skipped file rather than the whole run.

The gap between reading an id and opening the write transaction is two statements wide, and BEGIN IMMEDIATE waits on the 30-second busy timeout, so a concurrent rm holding the write lock holds that window open for as long as it likes. An insert against a deleted image_id violates the foreign key and throws, and parallel_for_each stops every worker on the first exception, so the cost of losing the race outside the transaction is the entire rebuild. Reading the id inside it means the write lock is already held and what was read cannot be deleted underneath it; a row that went before the transaction opened yields image_id < 0, a rollback and one recorded skip.

### R54 — holds (test gap)

A system SQLite compiled THREADSAFE=1 (serialized) mutexes every connection and the promise holds for free; one compiled THREADSAFE=2 (multi-thread) defaults to NOMUTEX, where sharing a connection is undefined and crashes rather than blocks. Asking for the flag means the ABI's promise does not depend on the packager's choice.

### R55 — holds

libphig's metadata writes take the writer lock without waiting and report PHIG_ERR_BUSY when it is held, and its long-running operations take no lock at all.

A GUI must not freeze behind a CLI job, so a contended lock is reported as an error the caller can surface rather than as a block — phig_acquire_write_lock passes no_wait = true, and PHIG_CATCH's LockBusy arm is the only path to PHIG_ERR_BUSY. The operations take none for a different reason: index's write set is unknowable before the walk, thumbs writes only the filesystem cache, and faces commits per image, so SQLite's own serialization is enough and small metadata writes stay serviceable for an operation's whole duration. A lock-holding operation would turn every tag write into PHIG_ERR_BUSY for the length of the run, which is the outcome this trade exists to avoid.

### R63 — holds

phig_last_error returns the calling thread's own last message, and only until that thread's next ABI call.

The storage is a function-local static thread_local std::string; PHIG_TRY clears it on entry and PHIG_CATCH sets it, so a later success on that thread wipes the message and a failure on another thread never appears in it. That is what lets a client drive one phig_ctx from several threads and still attribute an error to the call that produced it, which the handle-plus-poll operation model makes routine. The ctx argument is checked for null and otherwise ignored: the message is per-thread, not per-context, so two contexts used on one thread share the slot.

### R71 — holds (test gap)

A face row's embedding is written only by the insert that creates the row, so identify's `embedding = ?` clause refuses no write that `id = ?` and `person_id IS NULL` have not already refused.

Across core/, libphig/ and cli/ three statements update the faces table — `UPDATE faces SET image_id = ? WHERE image_id = ?` and the two that set person_id — and none of them writes embedding. The column is written by insert_face and by the v8 migration's `INSERT INTO faces_new (...) SELECT ... FROM faces`, both of which create rows rather than rewrite them. Re-detection is delete-and-reinsert — FacesEngine::run calls delete_faces_for_image then insert_face — which is also what keeps vec_faces in step, since it is keyed on faces.id, holds its own copy of the embedding, and is written only by those two functions. So the state this clause excludes, a row that keeps its id, stays unlabeled and carries a different embedding, is one phig cannot produce. The clause is kept deliberately: set_face_person_if_unchanged's header states it as the contract the caller wants, that the write refers to the face that was compared rather than to a row number, and as something that would catch an in-place embedding rewrite if one were added. Its cost is that phase 1 carries all 128 floats of every match into phase 2 to feed it, about 520 bytes per match where the id needs 8. Plan 044's work item 4 moves identify_person onto vec_faces KNN, which is where the choice lands: a KNN or paged phase 1 has to decide whether phase 2 still receives each matched embedding or only its id, and it cannot keep this clause without keeping the carry. 044 calls the transaction behaviour orthogonal to paging the read path, but that is about plan 031's phase split, not about this predicate's operands.

## cancellation

### R56 — holds (test gap)

Reconcile is not cancellable: run_reconcile takes no CancelToken, so a scan interrupted during its worker phase still relinks, demotes and deletes.

The phase mutates user-authored metadata inside one logged operation, and abandoning it halfway would leave the operation row stuck in_progress and the transfer passes half-applied — so it reads no token at all rather than reading one and ignoring it. That is why ScanEngine::run() is split: run_workers is cancellable, run_reconcile is not, and the split exists at exactly the boundary where a caller has to stop mapping a signal onto the token. cli/main.cpp destroys its ScopedInterruptHandler before calling run_reconcile so a Ctrl-C arriving during reconcile takes the default action instead of being silently swallowed. libphig never calls run_reconcile: the index operation is the additive half only.

| Protects | user-metadata, db-row, activity-log |
| Evidence | witness: `ScanEngine.ReconcileStillRunsAfterCancellation` |

### R57 — holds

Cancellation is polled only between whole items, so a run stopped by it leaves every item either fully done or untouched, and whatever committed before the stop stays committed.

parallel_for_each checks the token at the top of its work loop, before it claims the next index, so a worker never abandons an item it has started; scan, thumbs and faces inherit that by going through it. OrganizeEngine::apply has the same shape written by hand — the check is the first statement of its per-item loop, ahead of the destination re-check, execute_organize_action and carry_sidecars — so a cancellation cannot separate a media file from the attachment carried with it, even though a per-file error can (R48). Nothing is rolled back: rows and thumbnails already written stay, and the result reports completed = false, which is the only thing that distinguishes a stopped run from a finished one. The claim is about cancellation alone and is deliberately narrower than 'an item is never half done' — R33 records the disk-then-log window that no token controls.

### R58 — partial (test gap)

A run whose token is already cancelled does no work and reports itself incomplete.

The four cancellable engines answer this differently. ThumbsEngine and FacesEngine each guard the empty-selection path on purpose — thumbs with 'images.empty() ? !cancel.stop() : parallel_for_each(...)' and faces with a token check placed ahead of its empty-selection return — because parallel_for_each returns true unconditionally for a zero-length range and would otherwise report an already-cancelled run over nothing as completed. ScanEngine and OrganizeEngine have no such guard: run_workers assigns result.completed only inside 'if (!files.empty())' and apply only inside its per-item loop, so a cancelled scan of a directory holding no media files, and a cancelled apply of an empty plan, both return completed = true. Through the ABI that is the difference between PHIG_OP_DONE and PHIG_OP_CANCELLED, since both spawn wrappers derive the terminal state from that flag. Read from the code and corroborated by the test asymmetry — thumbs and faces each have an empty-selection case, scan and organize have none — not measured, because nothing outside the engines can produce an already-cancelled run over an empty selection on demand. The claim is provisional: 056 is the open plan that owns what an operation reports about its own status, and it does not name this.

### R67 — holds

phig_op_free joins the operation's worker rather than detaching it, so no engine thread outlives the handle or the Database it writes through.

The worker holds raw pointers to the phig_op and to the per-operation Database the handle owns, so returning while it still runs would leave it writing through freed memory — a use-after-free onto a live SQLite connection, which is the shape of corruption a client can neither see nor recover from. Joining makes phig_op_free block for as long as the item in flight takes; a caller that does not want to wait calls phig_op_cancel first, and cancellation lands between items (R57), so the wait is bounded by one item rather than by the run. phig_op_wait is the same join without the free.

### R20 — holds (test gap)

A dry-run removal takes no disk action, deletes no row and opens no logged operation, but it still creates the database file and applies any pending schema migration.

The preview returns before the confirmation guard and before log_begin_operation, so nothing on disk moves and nothing about the selection is recorded. What it does not skip is the connection: cmd_rm constructs a Database and calls init_schema before it reads dry_run, and both create-if-missing and the forward-only migration happen there. A preview that migrates a v7 database to v8 has changed the file it was asked not to touch, and no plan says so. This is the removal-shaped corner of the wider fact R70 records: every CLI command that opens a collection opens it read-write and migrates it, including the two operations.toml lists in read_only_cli. Database's read_only constructor flag exists and libphig uses it; cli/ never does.

### R59 — partial (test gap)

Whether a planned decision may be overridden is a property of the decision type: an organize conflict resolution may be changed by the caller before apply, and reconcile's deletions may not.

### R70 — violated (test gap)

A command that only reads a collection neither creates its database nor migrates its schema.

Every cli/ command that opens a collection opens it read-write. All twelve Database constructions in cli/main.cpp pass one argument, so all twelve take the default read_only = false, and cmd_search and cmd_duplicates then call init_schema on their first two lines (cli/main.cpp:855-856 and :500-501). Measured with the built binary: 'phig search --count' against a path holding no database left a 122880-byte file there whose meta table reads schema_version 8, then exited 1 with 'Database is empty.'; 'phig duplicates' against another such path did the same. Against copies of a two-image collection with meta.schema_version set back to 7, 'phig search --count' printed 2 and left the value at 8, and 'phig duplicates' left it at 8 as well. Under an empty XDG_DATA_HOME, 'phig help' and 'phig --help' created nothing, while 'phig search --count' with no --db created the database at the default path. Two consequences follow. A read migrates a collection forward irreversibly, and init_schema refuses a database newer than the build (core/database.cpp:301-305), so running search on one machine can make the collection unopenable by an older phig on another. And a mistyped --db leaves a stray empty collection behind instead of reporting that there is nothing there. R20 records the removal-shaped corner of this and R21 the organize-dry-run corner; both are scoped to a dry run, and this is the general fact. operations.toml's read_only_cli holds search, duplicates and help, and only help mutates nothing. Plan 043 owns it: the fix is a cli/ change — pass read_only on the commands that only read, and decide what they do with a database older than the build, which libphig answers with PHIG_ERR_SCHEMA — and 043 is the open plan that owns cli/, the same routing 060's open question 3 uses for cmd_organize's exit code. 054 cannot close it: 054 writes missing tests, and this needs the code to change.
